articles.title: Monolith vs Microservices: A Founder's Guide
articles.excerpt: Monolith vs microservices for founders: when one codebase wins, when splitting pays off, and the questions that settle the choice. Ask engineers whether to build a monolith or microservices and you wi…
articles.body: Monolith vs microservices for founders: when one codebase wins, when splitting pays off, and the questions that settle the choice. Ask engineers whether to build a monolith or microservices and you will get a confident answer in seconds. Ask again six months later, after the product has shipped and the team has grown, and the answer often changes. Monolith vs microservices has no permanently right answer. It depends on where your product is today, how big your team is, and what kind of pain you would rather deal with. Founders get caught out by this choice because it is usually presented as a technical one, when in reality it is a business one. The architecture you pick shapes how fast you can ship, how much a change costs, and how painful an outage becomes.

articles.title: Building a Private AI Control Plane for PS5 Porting: What We Learned After SQLite Locked Us Out at 2 AM
articles.excerpt: At 2:17 AM, the Open WebUI container restarted mid-upload. When it came back, the SQLite database was corrupted—conversations gone, user sessions dead. The root cause wasn't the restart. It was two op…
articles.body: At 2:17 AM, the Open WebUI container restarted mid-upload. When it came back, the SQLite database was corrupted—conversations gone, user sessions dead. The root cause wasn't the restart. It was two operators uploading PS5 executables simultaneously while the UI tried to write chat history to the same file. SQLite doesn't handle concurrent writes gracefully, and mounting the host filesystem directly into the container meant there was no write buffering, no transaction isolation, and no recovery path. That incident, combined with an earlier exposure where an admin panel became internet-accessible through a misconfigured reverse proxy default route, forced a architectural redesign. The problem wasn't Open WebUI.

articles.title: TypeScript errors in plain English: TS2307, TS2339, TS2532, TS2322 and friends
articles.excerpt: TypeScript's error messages are precise, but they're written for the compiler, not for you. Here are the ones that come up constantly, what they actually mean in plain English, and the fix that's usua…
articles.body: TypeScript's error messages are precise, but they're written for the compiler, not for you. Here are the ones that come up constantly, what they actually mean in plain English, and the fix that's usually right. TS2307: Cannot find module 'x' or its corresponding type declarations TypeScript can't find either the package or its types. npm install x # the package itself is missing npm install -D @types/x # the package has no bundled types For path aliases ( @/components/... ), the alias must be in tsconfig.json compilerOptions.paths and in your bundler config. For CSS, image or SVG imports, add a declaration file such as declare module "*.svg"; . TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module 'x' The package exists but ships no types and there's no @types/x .

articles.excerpt: How long to build a mobile app in 2026? A realistic timeline from idea to App Store launch, the phases, the delays, and the shortcuts that move the date. If you are planning an app, the timeline is us…
articles.body: How long to build a mobile app in 2026? A realistic timeline from idea to App Store launch, the phases, the delays, and the shortcuts that move the date. If you are planning an app, the timeline is usually the first question you ask and the hardest one to answer honestly. So here is the direct answer to how long to build a mobile app in 2026: a simple app typically takes two to three months, a mid-complexity app takes four to six months, and a large app with multiple user roles, payments, and integrations can take six months to a year. Most apps people actually ship land somewhere in the middle of that range. That range is wide because the calendar is rarely decided by how fast someone can write code.

articles.excerpt: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. Here's why Venus Express mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express. Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years. During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole . It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes . Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras . These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere. Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this.

articles.title: Who is King Ghidorah? The cosmic connections of Godzilla Minus Zero's foe
articles.excerpt: Godzilla will go toe-to-toe with long-time foe King Ghidorah in Godzilla Minus Zero. This three-headed Kaiju's origins aren't just space-based; one of the largest structures in the universe shares its…
articles.body: Godzilla goes toe-to-toe with long-time foe King Ghidorah in Godzilla Minus Zero, which opened in theaters on Friday (Nov. 6). Though the three-headed golden Kaiju might seem like a natural native of Monster Island, King Ghidorah actually emerged from the depths of space. However, it isn't just the origins of King Ghidorah — also known as Monster Zero in the Godzilla movie Invasion of Astro-Monster (1965) — that are this beast's only cosmic connection. One of the largest structures in the universe, the King Ghidorah Supercluster , was named in honor of Godzilla's primary antagonist. Eat that, King Kong!

articles.body: If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove. Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles.
